name: geography_set2_p1
label: Geography: set 2 (drainage, weather and climate, vegetation, soils, population and settlement)

papers.title: Drainage Systems and Hydrology: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on drainage systems and hydrology, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries is called a
questions.explanation:
A drainage basin (catchment) is all the land from which water flows into a river system.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- watershed: The watershed is the boundary of a drainage basin.
- confluence: A confluence is where two rivers meet.
- flood plain: A flood plain is flat land beside a river that floods.

questions.stem: The high ground that separates two neighbouring drainage basins is the
questions.explanation:
Rain falling on either side of a watershed flows into different river systems.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- source: The source is where a river begins.
- mouth: The mouth is where a river ends.
- tributary: A tributary is a smaller river that joins a main river.

questions.stem: A drainage pattern that looks like the branches of a tree is described as
questions.explanation:
Dendritic patterns develop on rocks of uniform resistance, where tributaries join at acute angles.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- trellised: Trellised patterns meet at right angles on alternating hard and soft rocks.
- radial: Radial streams flow outwards from a central high point.
- centripetal: Centripetal streams flow inwards into a basin.

questions.stem: A radial drainage pattern is most likely to develop on
questions.explanation:
Streams flow outwards in all directions from a central high point such as a volcano.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a basin surrounded by hills: A basin produces a centripetal pattern.
- alternating bands of hard and soft rock: That produces a trellised pattern.
- a flat plain of uniform rock: That usually produces a dendritic pattern.

options.label: B
options.content: alternating bands of hard and soft rock

options.label: C
options.content: a flat plain of uniform rock

questions.stem: The process by which water soaks from the ground surface into the soil is
questions.explanation:
Infiltration is one stage of the water cycle; water then moves through the soil and rocks as groundwater.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- evaporation: Evaporation turns water into water vapour.
- transpiration: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plants.
- condensation: Condensation turns water vapour into droplets.

papers.title: Weather and Climate: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on weather and climate, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Climate is best defined as
questions.explanation:
Weather is short-term; climate is the long-term average of weather conditions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the state of the atmosphere at a place at a given time: That is weather.
- the amount of rain that falls in one day: That is daily rainfall, one element of weather.
- the study of rocks and landforms: That is geomorphology.

options.label: A
options.content: the state of the atmosphere at a place at a given time

options.label: B
options.content: the average weather conditions of an area over a long period, usually 30 years or more

options.label: C
options.content: the amount of rain that falls in one day

options.label: D
options.content: the study of rocks and landforms

questions.stem: Relative humidity is measured with
questions.explanation:
The difference between the wet-bulb and dry-bulb readings gives the relative humidity from tables.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a barometer: A barometer measures air pressure.
- an anemometer: An anemometer measures wind speed.
- a rain gauge: A rain gauge measures rainfall.

questions.stem: Rainfall caused when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier is called
questions.explanation:
As air rises over high ground it cools, condenses and gives heavy rain on the windward side, as on the Freetown Peninsula.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- convectional rainfall: Convectional rain is caused by surface heating.
- frontal (cyclonic) rainfall: Frontal rain forms where warm and cold air masses meet.
- acid rain: Acid rain is polluted rain, not a type formed by rising air.

questions.stem: Lines drawn on a map to join places of equal atmospheric pressure are called
questions.explanation:
Isobars show pressure patterns; winds blow from high to low pressure.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- isotherms: Isotherms join places of equal temperature.
- isohyets: Isohyets join places of equal rainfall.
- contours: Contours join places of equal height.

questions.stem: A wind vane is used to show
questions.explanation:
Winds are named after the direction they come from; the vane's arrow points into the wind.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the speed of the wind: Wind speed is measured with an anemometer.
- the amount of water vapour in the air: Humidity is measured with a hygrometer.
- the pressure of the air: Pressure is measured with a barometer.

options.label: B
options.content: the direction from which the wind blows

options.label: C
options.content: the amount of water vapour in the air

papers.title: Climate Types: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on climate types, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A climate with high temperatures and rain in every month of the year is
questions.explanation:
Equatorial regions such as the Congo Basin are hot and wet all year, with a small annual temperature range.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Mediterranean climate: Mediterranean summers are dry.
- the hot desert climate: Deserts have very little rain.
- the tropical continental (savanna) climate: The savanna climate has a long dry season.

questions.stem: A characteristic of the hot desert climate is
questions.explanation:
Clear skies let the ground heat strongly by day and lose heat quickly at night.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- heavy rainfall all year: Deserts receive under 250 mm a year.
- high humidity: Desert air is very dry.
- cool, cloudy days: Desert days are hot and clear.

options.label: D
options.content: a very large daily range of temperature

questions.stem: The Mediterranean climate is characterised by
questions.explanation:
It is found at the northern and southern tips of Africa, around the Mediterranean and at the Cape.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- rain throughout the year: That describes the equatorial climate.
- hot, wet summers and dry winters: That describes the tropical wet-and-dry climate.
- very cold winters with snow: Mediterranean winters are mild.

options.label: A
options.content: hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters

options.label: C
options.content: hot, wet summers and dry winters

questions.stem: In the tropical wet-and-dry (savanna) climate, most rain falls
questions.explanation:
As the overhead sun and the ITCZ move into the savanna, moist winds bring the rainy season.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in winter, from the westerlies: Winter rain is typical of the Mediterranean climate.
- evenly in every month: That describes the equatorial climate.
- only during the harmattan: The harmattan is a dry wind.

options.label: B
options.content: in summer, when the sun is overhead

questions.stem: The Jos Plateau is cooler than Lagos mainly because of its
questions.explanation:
Temperature falls by about 6 °C for every 1,000 m of height, and the Jos Plateau is over 1,000 m high.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- distance from the Equator: Jos is not far enough north for latitude alone to explain the difference.
- heavier rainfall: Rainfall does not explain the lower temperatures.
- cold ocean current: Jos is far inland.

papers.title: Natural Vegetation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on natural vegetation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Trees of the tropical rainforest are
questions.explanation:
Heavy rain and high temperatures all year support dense, layered, evergreen forest.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- short and thorny with small leaves: That describes Sahel and desert vegetation.
- deciduous, losing their leaves in a cold winter: There is no cold winter in the rainforest.
- scattered among tall grasses: That describes the savanna.

options.label: A
options.content: short and thorny with small leaves

options.label: B
options.content: deciduous, losing their leaves in a cold winter

options.label: D
options.content: tall, evergreen and arranged in layers

questions.stem: Tall grass with scattered trees such as the shea and locust bean is typical of the
questions.explanation:
The Guinea savanna lies north of the forest, with tall grass and scattered trees.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sahel savanna: The Sahel has short grass and thorny scrub.
- mangrove swamp: Mangroves grow on tidal coasts.
- tropical rainforest: The rainforest has dense trees, not open grassland.

questions.stem: Mangrove trees are adapted to their environment by having
questions.explanation:
Mangroves grow in tidal estuaries; stilt roots anchor them and breathing roots take in air.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- thick bark to resist frequent fires: Fire resistance is typical of savanna trees.
- small, needle-like leaves to resist cold: Mangroves grow in hot tropical coasts.
- very deep tap roots to reach groundwater in deserts: That describes desert plants.

options.label: A
options.content: thick bark to resist frequent fires

options.label: B
options.content: stilt roots and breathing roots in salty, waterlogged mud

options.label: C
options.content: small, needle-like leaves to resist cold

options.label: D
options.content: very deep tap roots to reach groundwater in deserts

questions.stem: Short grass and thorny scrub along the southern edge of the Sahara form the
questions.explanation:
The Sahel receives about 250–500 mm of rain, enough only for short grass and thorny bushes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Guinea savanna: The Guinea savanna has tall grass and more trees.
- Sudan savanna: The Sudan savanna lies between the Guinea and Sahel savannas.
- montane forest: Montane forest grows on high mountains.

questions.stem: Plants adapted to survive in very dry conditions are called
questions.explanation:
Xerophytes have features such as deep roots, small or waxy leaves and water storage.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- hydrophytes: Hydrophytes grow in water.
- halophytes: Halophytes are adapted to salty conditions.
- epiphytes: Epiphytes grow on other plants, as in the rainforest.

papers.title: Soils: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on soils, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In a soil profile, the horizon where materials washed down from the topsoil accumulate is the
questions.explanation:
Leached minerals and clay are deposited in the subsoil, the B horizon.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A horizon (topsoil): The A horizon is the zone that loses material by leaching.
- C horizon: The C horizon is weathered parent rock.
- O horizon: The O horizon is the layer of organic litter on top.

questions.stem: The removal of soluble minerals from the topsoil by water moving downwards is called
questions.explanation:
Heavy tropical rainfall washes plant nutrients down out of reach of roots, lowering fertility.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- weathering: Weathering breaks down rock; it does not move minerals.
- capillary action: Capillary action moves water upwards.
- humification: Humification is the formation of humus from organic matter.

questions.stem: Lateritic soils in the tropics are formed mainly by
questions.explanation:
Heavy rain and high temperatures remove silica and bases, leaving red iron-rich soils that can harden into laterite.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- deposition of fine material by the wind: Wind-blown deposits form loess.
- deposition of silt by rivers: River deposits form alluvial soils.
- freezing and thawing in cold climates: Laterites form in hot, wet climates.

options.label: A
options.content: deposition of fine material by the wind

options.label: C
options.content: heavy leaching that leaves iron and aluminium oxides near the surface

options.label: D
options.content: freezing and thawing in cold climates

questions.stem: Soil formed from material deposited by rivers on flood plains is called
questions.explanation:
Alluvial soils are fertile and are used for rice and vegetables in river valleys.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- lateritic soil: Lateritic soil forms by leaching on uplands.
- loess: Loess is deposited by the wind.
- sandy desert soil: Desert soils form in arid areas.

questions.stem: Which method helps to control soil erosion on hillsides?
questions.explanation:
Terraces and contour ridges slow runoff so that water soaks in instead of washing soil away.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ploughing up and down the slope: Furrows down the slope channel water and speed erosion.
- bush burning before planting: Burning exposes the soil to rain and wind.
- overgrazing by cattle: Overgrazing removes the vegetation cover.

options.label: B
options.content: ploughing up and down the slope

papers.title: Population: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on population, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A country has an area of 72,000 km² and a population of 7.2 million. Its population density is
questions.explanation:
Density = population ÷ area = 7,200,000 ÷ 72,000 = 100 persons per km².

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 10 persons per km²: That divides by 720,000 instead of 72,000.
- 1,000 persons per km²: That divides by 7,200 instead of 72,000.
- 0.01 persons per km²: That divides the area by the population.

questions.stem: A country's birth rate is 38 per 1,000 and its death rate is 11 per 1,000. Its rate of natural increase is
questions.explanation:
Natural increase = 38 − 11 = 27 per 1,000 = 2.7% per year.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.9%: That adds the death rate instead of subtracting it.
- 27%: 27 per 1,000 is 2.7%, not 27%.
- 0.27%: 27 per 1,000 is 2.7%, not 0.27%.

questions.stem: A population pyramid with a wide base and a narrow top shows
questions.explanation:
Many children at the base and few old people at the top is typical of developing countries such as Sierra Leone.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a low birth rate and an ageing population: That gives a narrow base.
- more males than females: The sexes are shown on the two sides, not by the shape of the base.
- a falling population: A wide base shows many births, so the population is growing.

options.label: A
options.content: a low birth rate and an ageing population

options.label: D
options.content: a high birth rate and a young population

questions.stem: Which of the following is a push factor of rural–urban migration?
questions.explanation:
Push factors drive people away from their home area; pull factors attract them to towns.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- better schools and hospitals in towns: This attracts people, so it is a pull factor.
- higher wages in towns: This is a pull factor.
- relatives already living in the town: This is a pull factor.

options.label: A
options.content: lack of jobs and amenities in villages

options.label: B
options.content: better schools and hospitals in towns

options.label: D
options.content: relatives already living in the town

questions.stem: A population census is
questions.explanation:
A census records the number, age, sex and other details of everyone in the country, usually every ten years.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a survey of a sample of households: A sample survey does not count everyone.
- the registration of births and deaths: That is vital registration.
- a count of voters before an election: That is voter registration.

options.label: A
options.content: a survey of a sample of households

options.label: B
options.content: an official count of all the people in a country at a given time

options.label: C
options.content: the registration of births and deaths

options.label: D
options.content: a count of voters before an election

papers.title: Settlement Patterns: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on settlement patterns, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A settlement in which the houses are clustered closely together is described as
questions.explanation:
Nucleated settlements grow around a centre such as a chief's compound, market or water point.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- dispersed: Dispersed houses are scattered over the land.
- linear: Linear settlements stretch along a road, river or coast.
- isolated: An isolated dwelling stands alone.

questions.stem: Linear settlements usually develop along
questions.explanation:
People build along routes and water to gain access to transport, trade and water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the tops of steep mountains: Steep mountain tops discourage settlement.
- swamps far from routes: Swamps far from routes are avoided.
- the centre of large forests: Forest centres lack routes for a line of houses.

questions.stem: The actual land on which a settlement is built is its
questions.explanation:
Site factors include water supply, dry land, defence and flat land.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- situation: Situation is its position in relation to the surrounding area.
- hinterland: The hinterland is the area served by a settlement.
- function: Function is the main activity of the settlement.

questions.stem: The minimum number of customers needed to keep a service in business is its
questions.explanation:
High-order services such as universities need a large threshold population.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- range: Range is the maximum distance people will travel to use a service.
- sphere of influence: The sphere of influence is the area a settlement serves.
- hierarchy: Hierarchy is the ranking of settlements by size and importance.

questions.stem: Koidu in Sierra Leone grew mainly as a
questions.explanation:
Koidu, in Kono District, grew after diamonds were discovered there in the 1930s.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- port town: Koidu is far inland, not on the coast.
- religious centre: Koidu did not grow around a religious centre.
- national capital: Freetown is the national capital.

papers.title: Urbanization: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on urbanization, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Urbanization means
questions.explanation:
A country urbanizes when the percentage of its people living in urban areas rises.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the building of roads between towns: Road building is not urbanization.
- the movement of people from towns to villages: That is counter-urbanization.
- the growth of farming around towns: That is peri-urban agriculture.

options.label: A
options.content: the building of roads between towns

options.label: B
options.content: the movement of people from towns to villages

options.label: C
options.content: the growth of farming around towns

options.label: D
options.content: an increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pull factor attracting migrants to towns?
questions.explanation:
Pull factors are the attractions of towns: jobs, amenities, security and city life.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- poor harvests in rural areas: This pushes people out of rural areas.
- land shortage in villages: This is a push factor.
- insecurity in rural areas: This is a push factor.

options.label: A
options.content: better social amenities such as schools, hospitals and electricity

questions.stem: The part of a city with the highest land values, offices, banks and shops is the
questions.explanation:
Competition for central, accessible land makes the CBD the most expensive part of a city.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- rural–urban fringe: The fringe is on the edge of the city where land is cheaper.
- industrial zone: Industry usually lies along transport routes away from the centre.
- outer residential zone: Outer suburbs are mainly housing.

questions.stem: A major problem caused by rapid urbanization in West African cities is
questions.explanation:
Migrants who cannot afford housing build shacks on unplanned land, as at Kroo Bay and Susan's Bay in Freetown.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a shortage of farm labour in towns: Towns do not depend on farm labour.
- the decline of urban markets: Urban markets grow with population.
- a fall in traffic: Traffic increases as cities grow.

options.label: A
options.content: a shortage of farm labour in towns

options.label: C
options.content: the growth of slums and informal settlements

questions.stem: Which measure would best reduce rural–urban migration?
questions.explanation:
Rural development reduces push factors, so fewer people need to move to the cities.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- building more factories in the capital city: This attracts even more migrants to the capital.
- raising wages only in towns: Higher urban wages pull more people to towns.
- closing rural schools: This would push more people to towns.

options.label: A
options.content: building more factories in the capital city

options.label: D
options.content: providing jobs and amenities in rural areas
